title: Notebook-First and Script-First Workflow
content:
## Choose a workflow

A notebook keeps code, written reasoning and displayed results in one document. A Python script runs a saved sequence of statements. Use a notebook for short exploratory steps and an explanation beside each result; use a script when the same calculation needs a repeatable run. Both workflows need the input, code and assumptions that produced the result.

The site IDE runs Python scripts and retains project files. Its console is not a Jupyter notebook kernel. A notebook workflow uses a notebook application such as Jupyter or Colab. Native scripts run through a local Python interpreter. Record which workflow and Python version produced an output; success in one environment does not establish success in another.

## Keep the input with the code

For a small analysis, keep `main.py` or `analysis.ipynb`, an unchanged input in `data/`, a short `README.md` and separately generated outputs. A filename alone does not identify a dataset version, so retain the exact input used. Keep raw data distinct from cleaned data.

In a notebook, restart the kernel and run the cells from the top. In a script, start a new Python process and run the saved file. Compare the resulting values with a small hand calculation. A displayed result left from an earlier execution is evidence about that earlier execution.

## Worked setup check

The same six trip counts, `2, 4, 8, 0, 6, 12`, have count 6, total 32 and mean about 5.33 trips per record. Record the count and unit alongside the mean. A reproducible calculation can still have a limited interpretation: these synthetic observations describe no real population.

title: Data Science in Python Core Concepts
content:
The course begins with core Python: variables, sequences, loops, functions and reading text files. Its central work is descriptive analysis: understanding a question, inspecting and cleaning input, calculating summaries, visualizing evidence and communicating a conclusion within the data's limits. Predictive modeling has a separate purpose in Machine Learning.

Install packages when an activity needs them. The opening arithmetic, CSV and reproducibility exercises use Python's standard library. Later DataFrame work introduces pandas; numerical-array work uses NumPy; static charts use Matplotlib. A console dashboard can use ordinary input and printing. Altair, Streamlit and scikit-learn are not prerequisites for every project.

For native work, create a project-specific virtual environment. On macOS or Linux:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"
```

On Windows:

```powershell
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"
```

Use that same environment's Python when installing a required package and running the project. Follow the selected project's dependency instructions and retain the versions used. The site IDE manages its browser runtime separately; these terminal commands apply to native Python.

A useful setup check runs a small program, saves it, closes it and runs the saved version again. Preserve its input, output and Python version. The [Python virtual-environment guide](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html) describes the environment commands.

title: Core Project: Data Science in Python
content:
Create a small analysis workspace and verify that saved code can reproduce a known result. Keep a script named `main.py`, a `README.md` stating the workflow and Python version, and a `data/` folder reserved for retained input files.

Place this complete first calculation in `main.py`:

```python
trips = [2, 4, 8, 0, 6, 12]
count = len(trips)
total = sum(trips)
mean = total / count if count else None
print(f"Records: {count}")
print(f"Total trips: {total}")
print("Mean trips per record: " + (f"{mean:.2f}" if mean is not None else "undefined"))
```

The expected three lines are `Records: 6`, `Total trips: 32` and `Mean trips per record: 5.33`. Check the total by hand. Save the file and rerun it from a fresh script process or a restarted notebook kernel. A notebook version uses the same statements in a code cell, with the hand calculation in a Markdown cell.

Change the final value from 12 to 18. Predict the new total 38 and displayed mean 6.33 before running. Save this as a separate checkpoint so the original version remains available.

**Verification:** Retain both code versions, their observed outputs, the hand checks and the environment note. Explain that the results summarize six synthetic records and do not measure a real site's typical traffic.

title: Reference Archive: Data Science in Python Workspace
content:
The [Data Science source repository](https://github.com/instruction-material/Data-Science) contains the course's project folders. Use the starter or reference attached to the selected activity; the repository root is an archive of multiple projects.

A starter contains an unfinished part for the assigned task. A reference provides one completed implementation for comparison after an attempt. A repository-wide download can include unrelated packages and exercises, so retain the exact selected folder and its supplied data when recording a result.

Keep an earlier working copy before trying a new variant. Record the source revision or download date with the project. A link to an archive establishes where material can be found; the assigned lesson establishes the question, expected behavior and evidence required.

title: Data Science in Python Setup Transfer Practice
content:
Repeat the setup calculation using the new values `1, 1, 4, 10`. Create a separate saved copy, predict the count, total and mean, then run it using the same workflow as the core project.

Expected values are count 4, total 16 and mean 4.00. Verify that the output's denominator is four records rather than the original six. Reopen the original version and check that its values and output remain unchanged.

Record the input, observed output, Python version and location of each saved version. Explain which parts of the program stayed the same and why the mean changed. Changing data while retaining the same calculation is the transfer being checked; switching editors is optional.

title: Data Science in Python Setup Extension Practice
content:
Extend the setup calculation with two separate inputs: an empty list and one list containing a recorded zero, `[0]`.

Before running, predict both outcomes. Empty input has count 0, total 0 and an undefined mean. One recorded zero has count 1, total 0 and mean 0.00. The conditional expression in the core example prevents division by zero while preserving this distinction.

Save and rerun both cases. Keep the printed count beside the result and explain why an undefined mean cannot be reported as an observed zero. Retain these boundary checks with the original six-record calculation.

title: What Data Science Is Core Concepts
content:
## Ask a descriptive question

A descriptive question names the records being compared and the quantity to calculate. “Which synthetic site has the largest total trip count in these records?” is answerable from the complete table below. “Which real site is busiest?” needs evidence about sampling, time and exposure that this fixture does not provide.

## Worked comparison

| Site | Trips |
| --- | ---: |
| north | 2 |
| north | 4 |
| south | 8 |
| west | 0 |
| west | 6 |
| west | 12 |

Each row is one synthetic observation. A repeated site label represents another observation, not automatically a duplicate error. A recorded zero is a value. A missing value would require a separate rule and explanation.

North totals 6 trips across two records, south totals 8 across one, and west totals 18 across three. West has the largest recorded total. The per-record means are north 3.00, south 8.00 and west 6.00, so south has the largest mean. The two rankings answer different questions.

## Interpret the result

An analysis connects its question, source, calculation, result and limitation. A chart can communicate that chain, but cannot supply missing evidence. A larger sample or a fitted model also needs a defined question and suitable evidence. This course emphasizes descriptive work; an AI search procedure or a predictive model changes the main task and evaluation.

title: Core Project: What Data Science Is
content:
Write a question-and-evidence brief for the six synthetic observations in the lesson. This is a written analysis; code is optional for checking arithmetic.

Choose either total trips by site or mean trips per recorded observation. State the question, unit represented by one row, columns used, calculation and audience. Work out every site's result by hand before choosing how to display it.

For totals, expected values are north 6, south 8 and west 18. For means, use the matching record counts: north 2, south 1 and west 3, giving 3.00, 8.00 and 6.00 trips per record. Check that group counts sum to 6 and group totals sum to 32.

Write one supported conclusion using the words “synthetic records.” Then identify a stronger real-world claim these records cannot establish and the missing evidence needed to assess it. A useful brief makes the denominator and scope visible without requiring a reader to inspect code.

title: Analysis Log: What Data Science Is
content:
Keep an analysis log for the question-and-evidence brief. Record the precise question, retained six-row input, row meaning, columns and units, chosen calculation, hand-check result and limitation.

Add two entries: the initial plan and the completed calculation. If the question or denominator changes, record why and which earlier result is affected. Separate an observed result such as west's recorded total 18 from an interpretation such as a claim about real traffic.

**Verification:** Another reader can trace one reported number back to the listed records, identify what changed between entries and find a limitation that affects the conclusion. This log records decisions and evidence; it does not require a separate program or a repeated copy of the report.

title: Transfer Practice: What Data Science Is
content:
Transfer the descriptive question to these four synthetic observations: east has trip counts 1 and 5; west has trip counts 4 and 4.

Write two questions, one comparing totals and one comparing means. Both sites total 6 and 8 respectively, with means 3.00 and 4.00. Check count 4 and overall total 14. State whether the same site leads under both questions.

Compare this case with the lesson's original six observations, where the largest total and largest mean belonged to different sites. Explain how equal group sizes affect the relationship between total and mean rankings. The exercise supports a numerical observation about the given records, rather than a general claim that group sizes are always equal.

title: Extension Practice: What Data Science Is
content:
Assess the claim “West is the busiest site” using the lesson's six synthetic observations. Identify at least two possible meanings of busiest, such as largest recorded total or largest mean per observation, and calculate each relevant result.

Rewrite the claim so its quantity, input and scope are explicit. Then propose one additional measurement that would support a different question: a common observation period, a defined sampling rule or an exposure measure. Describe how that measurement would enter the comparison.

**Verification:** The response distinguishes the west total 18 from the south mean 8.00, retains each group's record count and explains why proposed future evidence is not an observed result. The deliverable is a claim critique and revised question.

title: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility Core Concepts
content:
## Recognize hidden state

A notebook kernel stores values from executed cells. The displayed order of cells can differ from the order they were executed. This creates hidden state when a later result depends on a value that the saved top-to-bottom sequence does not reproduce.

## Worked example

Consider two cells in this order:

```python
# Cell 1
trips = [2, 4, 8]
```

```python
# Cell 2
print(sum(trips))
```

A fresh top-to-bottom run prints 14. If Cell 1 is changed to `[2, 4, 8, 0, 6, 12]` and Cell 2 is run without first rerunning Cell 1, the kernel still holds the earlier list and can print 14. The correct new total is 32. Saving edited text does not by itself execute it.

## Verify a fresh run

After a meaningful change, restart the kernel and run the saved cells in order. In a script workflow, run the saved script in a new process. Record the exact input and environment, compare an output with a hand calculation and keep the explanation beside the result.

File location is another dependency. A script can find bundled data relative to its own `__file__`; a notebook usually needs a documented working directory or an explicit input path. A path that works in one editor session can fail when another person launches from elsewhere. The [Jupyter notebook documentation](https://jupyter-notebook.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebook.html) describes the relationship between saved cells, execution and kernel state.

title: Core Project: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility
content:
Build a reproducible small analysis that reads the supplied six-row `data/sample.csv`, calculates record count, total trips and mean, and prints the result with its units. Keep the raw CSV unchanged.

Open the starter in the course IDE and complete `summarize(values)`. Run `main.py` with the bundled input. In a local terminal, run `python main.py` from the starter folder. The script locates the CSV beside the saved file. A notebook version records its input path and places loading before calculation in the visible cell sequence.

Predict count 6, total 32 and mean 5.33. Run from a fresh process or restarted kernel, then repeat without editing input or code. Compare both results with the hand check. Also launch the native script from a different working directory using its full path; the bundled input must still be found.

Copy `data/sample.csv` to `data/changed.csv` and change the last value from 12 to 18. In a terminal, rerun with `python main.py --input data/changed.csv`. From a notebook, pass the same input path to `main`. Predict count 6, total 38 and mean 6.33. Retain the original and changed inputs with their distinct output records.

**Verification:** The saved artifact includes code, both retained inputs, run instructions, environment information and the observed comparisons. A missing input produces a visible error rather than silently substituting another dataset.

title: Analysis Log: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility
content:
Create a run log for the reproducibility project. Each entry names the saved code version, exact input path or retained input version, Python environment, launch method, observed count/total/mean and hand-check result.

Include the fresh default run, a second unchanged run, launch from another working directory and the changed-input run. For a notebook, additionally record the restart-and-run-all result. For a script-only workflow, mark notebook execution as outside that run's scope.

Separate experiments from established steps. An exploratory edited cell becomes part of the reproducible analysis only after the saved ordered sequence produces its result from a fresh start. Record any mismatch and the correction that resolves it.

title: Transfer Practice: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility
content:

Run `python main.py --input data/empty.csv` and `python main.py --input data/zero.csv` from the project folder. Expect empty input to have zero records, total zero and no measured mean. Repeat the runs from a fresh process or restarted notebook kernel. Record each input with its output and explain how explicitly selecting the input prevents an earlier dataset from silently remaining in use. The transfer checks a changed data condition while retaining the analysis sequence.

title: Extension Practice: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility
content:
Complete `write_report(output, summary, input_path)` in the supplied extension starter. The report records the SHA-256 digest of the selected CSV bytes alongside the filename and results. The report identifies the retained input, count, total, mean or undefined-mean state, and the units used. Keep the source CSV unchanged and store generated output separately.

Run `python main.py`, reopen `outputs/report.json` and compare each number with the console and hand calculation. Copy the CSV to `data/changed.csv` and replace its last value with 18. Run `python main.py --input data/changed.csv --output outputs/changed.json` to retain both reports. The new report must contain total 38 and mean 6.33, rather than retaining the earlier 32 and 5.33.

Record what generated the report and which earlier report was retained or replaced. A fresh rerun with the same input reproduces its numerical content. A report's existence alone does not establish that it came from the current input.

title: pandas Foundations Core Concepts
content:
## Inspect the input

One row in the practice CSV represents one synthetic trip record. `trip_id` identifies it, `site` names its site, and `trips` and `hours` are whole-number measurements. Start with a question: what is the mean number of trips per record at each site?

```csv
trip_id,site,trips,hours
R01,north,2,1
R02,north,4,2
R03,south,8,4
R04,west,0,0
R05,west,6,3
R06,west,12,3
```

Save the table as `data/sample.csv` in a script's working folder, or use the supplied copy in the project. Inspect the table before calculating:

```python
import pandas as pd

frame = pd.read_csv("data/sample.csv")
print(frame.shape, frame.columns.tolist())
print(frame.head(3))
print(frame.dtypes)
```

Expect six rows, four columns and IDs R01 through R03 in the preview. Identify which field is the group and which field is measured. This dataset has no missing observations. The recorded zero is part of the west total and denominator.

## Worked selection and grouping

`frame.loc[frame["trips"].ge(6), ["trip_id", "trips"]]` keeps R03, R05 and R06 in source order. Sorting can change their order without changing which records match. A separate grouping uses all six rows and combines each site's observations:

```python
groups = frame.groupby("site", as_index=False).agg(
    records=("trips", "size"),
    total_trips=("trips", "sum"),
    mean_trips=("trips", "mean"),
)
print(groups)
```

## Explain the denominators

North is 6 ÷ 2 = 3, south is 8 ÷ 1 = 8, and west is 18 ÷ 3 = 6. South's mean comes from one record, so the counts belong beside the means. For a different question, divide each row's trips by its hours only when hours is nonzero. R04 has an undefined rate. A measured rate of zero instead requires recorded zero trips and positive hours.

[CSV input in pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html) · [Grouping in pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/groupby.html)

In a separate input copy, change R01 to zero trips with one hour and check that its rate is now 0, while R04 is still undefined. title: Cleaning and Validation Core Concepts
content:
The question for this module is how many trips are supported by valid, distinct records. Start by preserving the raw table. A cleaning audit records one outcome per input record so each inclusion and exclusion can be inspected.

```csv
trip_id,site,trips,hours
R01, North ,2,1
R02,north,4,2
R02,NORTH,4,2
R03,south,,4
R04,west,nope,0
R05,west,-1,3
R06,west,0,0
R07,west,12,3
R08,,3,1
R09,East,6,3
```

Read initially as text. This preserves a blank and a malformed number as different evidence. For the provided CSV, inspect the original numeric text before classifying:

```python
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.read_csv("data/sample.csv", dtype="string", keep_default_na=False)
trips_text = raw["trips"].str.strip()
numeric = pd.to_numeric(trips_text, errors="coerce")
missing = trips_text.eq("")
malformed = ~missing & numeric.isna()
outside_range = (numeric.lt(0) | numeric.gt(1000)).fillna(False)
print(raw.loc[missing | malformed | outside_range, ["trip_id", "trips"]])
```

This preview identifies R03, R04 and R05. The full project also validates whole numbers, checks hours from 0 through 24, and accepts site labels east, north, south or west after the declared repair. If fields fail in the same row, record the first outcome in ID, site, trips, then hours order. Zero is allowed. R08 has a missing site even though it has a recorded trip count.

Trim and lowercase known labels before comparing valid rows that share a trip ID. The two R02 rows then agree, so keep the first and count the second as a duplicate. When the same ID has two different valid measurements, hold both for review. This policy protects the distinct-record total from a guess about which measurement is correct.

Check the accounting: 10 original rows = 5 accepted + 1 repeat + 4 invalid. Two accepted labels were repaired. The accepted total is 24 trips; that total describes the retained records and does not establish what the missing or invalid observations would have contributed.

[Numeric conversion in pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.to_numeric.html) · [Duplicate row selection in pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.duplicated.html)

title: Core Project: Cleaning and Validation
content:

Classify blanks as missing, invalid whole-number text as malformed, and parsed counts outside 0–1000 trips or 0–24 hours as out of range.

In a copy of the CSV, try a record with 25 hours or a blank hours field. Predict which outcome changes before rerunning the copy. Retain the original and changed input with their reports. Explain how one row can have several defects while the audit still accounts for it once.

content:

Reconcile accepted and excluded records to ten, and tie the total of 24 trips to the five accepted records. For one change to a rule, describe which original records might move between categories and what evidence would justify the change. Preserve the raw CSV so the comparison can be repeated.

title: Data Science in Python Reference Guide
content:
## Check a library operation

Use the documentation for the installed version when a method's defaults matter. In the [pandas documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/), look up the operation, its missing-value behavior, and one example. Try the smallest input that distinguishes the two outcomes before applying the operation to a whole table.

## Worked check

For a column containing 0, a missing value, and 6, the count of rows is three and the count of measured values is two. Averaging the measured values gives 3. Filling the missing value with zero first gives 2. Write down the rule you used and report the denominator alongside the mean.

When a decision affects people, record who is represented in the table and who might be absent. An analysis with a correct calculation can still support an overly broad claim.

title: Data Science in Python Core Skills
content:
## Evidence for each skill

- **Read a dataset.** Name the unit of observation, the column types, and the meaning of a missing value.
- **Validate a transformation.** Retain the raw file and reconcile the accepted and rejected rows.
- **Summarize a comparison.** Report the measurement, group size, and comparison window.
- **Communicate a result.** Choose a display that makes the comparison readable and explain one limitation.
- **Reproduce the result.** Run the saved analysis with identified inputs and compare the output with a separate check.

## Worked check

Site A has 2 and 4 trips. Site B has 8 trips in one record. A's mean is 3, B's is 8, and the mean across all records is 14 ÷ 3. Explain why the overall mean is different from the average of the two site means.

title: Data Science in Python Next Topics
content:
## Choose a question that extends the analysis

An exploratory analysis can lead to more careful measurement, a different graphical comparison, or a model. Pick the extension that would resolve an open question in the original report. A question about a seasonal pattern calls for comparable time windows. A question about differences between sites calls for checking coverage and group sizes.

## Worked extension

Suppose an observed trip count increases from 20 to 24. With one day of coverage in each period, the observed daily count rises by four. If the second period contains two days, its daily mean is 12. Add coverage dates before explaining what changed.

When the comparison is reproducible, consider statistical inference for a sampling question, or Machine Learning for a prediction question with a defined target and an independent evaluation set.

title: Data Science in Python Boundaries
content:
## What a descriptive report can support

State a claim about the records you analyzed. Identify the population you would need to observe to make a broader claim. For a comparison over time, check the coverage and how the measurement was collected. For a claim about causes, other plausible explanations and an appropriate study design matter.

## Worked boundary check

Suppose an event is followed by more bookings in the current table. Check how many days were observed on each side of the event and whether weekend days are represented equally. A defensible caption can report the observed comparison and name these differences as limits on the interpretation.

Use published example data or synthetic records for sharing. Before publishing working files, check the dataset terms and remove personal identifiers that the analysis can do without.

title: Data Science in Python Prerequisite Check
content:
Write the results of a four-row check before starting a spreadsheet or Python analysis. The input rows have trip counts 5, 0, blank, and 7. Record the row count, measured count, total, and mean of the measured values. Explain why the zero belongs in the denominator and the blank is treated separately. Recompute the mean after replacing the blank with zero, and state the assumption implicit in that decision.

Write one row of a data dictionary for this field. Include its name, units, valid values, and how the file signals a missing entry. Compare your two expected means with a hand calculation. Keep both results and explain which rule you would use with an unfamiliar source.

title: Data Science in Python Pathway Map
content:
Choose one next step from stronger data preparation, a clearer report, or an introductory prediction project. Start with a result you can already reproduce. Name the current input, the exact calculation or chart, and the evidence that it works. Write the new question and one prerequisite that the new work will need.

For example, a report of mean trips by site can lead to a comparison across weeks. Before combining weeks, identify the coverage dates and decide how a missing day will be recorded. Set a small success check, such as reconciling the observed day counts for each site. Deliver the question, prerequisite, and check together with a short explanation of why you chose this next step.

title: Data Science in Python Follow-Up Path
content:
## Build on a finished report

Keep one reproducible report as a baseline when moving to a harder problem. When the cleaning decisions are hard to explain, spend the next pass on data provenance and validation. When the comparison is difficult to read, revise the display or summarize the same measurement by a relevant group. When the question is predictive, write down the target and how the prediction would be evaluated on later observations.

## Worked choice

A transit report compares daily totals across routes. One route has fewer recorded days. A useful next project compares the number of observations per route and daily rates over a common period. Record the original result, the new question, and the specific evidence that changed the conclusion.

title: Data Science in Python Resource Map
content:
## Choose the material needed for the next action

Open **Learn** for explanations and worked examples. Use **Projects** for the central practice and **Supplemental Projects** for transfer and extension. A starter provides the initial files for a coding task. A dataset supplies the recorded values and their units. A reference implementation lets you check the behavior of a completed program.

## Worked choice

For a cleaning task, inspect the original CSV before modifying the starter. Use a worked example to decide what the rule should do. Compare the output from your solution with the expected row counts. Save the resulting code in the same project, then download a copy if it needs to run outside the site.

For an open-data project, record the publisher, date range, license or use terms, and any transformations alongside the copy you analyzed.

title: Data Science in Python Module Alignment Guide
content:
## Move from evidence to a report

| Section | Work to keep |
| --- | --- |
| Setup and notebook workflow | One rerun with recorded inputs and versions |
| pandas foundations | A table with named columns, types, and a checked calculation |
| Cleaning and validation | A decision log with original, accepted, and rejected counts |
| Visualization and statistics | A display with units and an interpretable comparison |
| Storytelling and dashboards | A claim tied to the data supporting it |
| Domain projects and capstone | A report another reader can reproduce |

## Worked transition

A clean table alone does not answer a question. After validating a column of trip counts, choose a comparison such as mean trips by site. Record each site's group size and explain whether the comparison describes a typical row or a typical site.

title: Data Science in Python Reference Map
content:
## Find a check for each stage

The Standards Map explains what a course result should establish. The practice guide helps choose a next project and review the work. Use the toolchain notes when an external Python setup needs the packages or file structure required by a project.

## Worked route

For a capstone that reports a mean by category, start with the earlier pandas example and save a tiny input whose result you can compute by hand. Consult cleaning and validation when fields are missing or duplicated. Review the matching chart example before writing a caption. Store the source, script, output, and assumptions together when you submit the report.

When a reference example has several files, compare the result with the source files it ran on. This makes it possible to tell whether a mismatch came from the code or the inputs.

title: Data Science in Python Prerequisite Map
content:
Trace the inputs to a proposed report for a new dataset. Name the observation unit, one comparison, and a useful final display. List what must exist before each step and how you will verify it. For example, a comparison of daily rates needs a measurement total and coverage days for each group. If one period has 40 trips across two days and another has 48 across four days, check the rates before designing the chart.

Mark the first missing prerequisite and add a concrete check that resolves it. Deliver a small dependency map plus two hand calculations whose answers a reader can reproduce. Point to the module where you would practice the missing skill.

title: Data Science in Python Resource Inventory
content:
Prepare a one-page inventory for an analysis another reader can rerun. Record the original data file and publisher, observation date range, fields used, script or notebook, package versions, and the report or chart that makes the claim. Give each file one role. Include how to start the analysis and how the reader can check one result independently.

Run the analysis once from the saved project or notebook and record the output of the check. For example, for a table of four measured counts 2, 5, 0, and 9, verify that the total is 16 and the mean is 4. Record whether that check used a supplied dataset or a separate test fixture. Keep dataset use terms with the inventory.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python Setup Assumptions
content:
## Record the runtime and inputs

A repeatable project records the Python version, the package versions it uses, the project revision, and the input filename. In Python, `sys.version` identifies the runtime. In a pandas project, `pandas.__version__` gives the installed pandas version. Read the project README for packages and the command that runs the script.

## Worked setup

Start with the supplied `data/sample.csv` for the reproducibility project. It has six measured rows with a total of 32 trips. A completed project should report six records, 32 total trips and a mean of 5.33. Save those three values with your runtime and package versions. An outside CSV can have a different schema or count, so use the supplied fixture to check setup first.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python Upgrade Rule
content:
## Compare results before changing versions

Keep a known-working copy of the starter, its input and its expected output. Try the new version in a separate environment and rerun the same input. Compare the actual output and warnings with the baseline. If a default changes, choose the behavior explicitly in the code and record it in the README.

## Worked upgrade

Suppose a date parser begins interpreting a field differently after a package update. Test a fixture containing `2026-02-01` and one invalid date. The valid value should represent February 1 and the invalid row should follow the project's error rule. Retain the previous environment until the new one passes the fixture and the full project.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python Platform Fallbacks
content:
## Pick a place to run the project

Use the course IDE for projects whose starter opens there. The IDE runs Python in the browser. To run an exported starter on a computer, preserve its folders, follow the README in a fresh environment, and install the dependencies the project names. Notebook and dashboard projects may require a local notebook or app runner listed in their instructions.

## Worked fallback

If the browser cannot load a package for a CSV project, download the starter ZIP and extract it with its `data/` folder. From the extracted project directory, run the README command on `data/sample.csv`. Compare the result with the lesson's expected summary. If the file cannot be found, check the working directory and the extracted path before changing the analysis.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python Reproducibility Notes
content:
## Keep enough information to rerun

Save the input file or a versioned source reference, the code or notebook, the run command, dependency versions and the expected result. Record assumptions about missing values, row coverage, units and grouping alongside the result. A chart alone leaves out the rules that produced it.

## Worked note

A saved site-summary project uses `data/sample.csv` and groups measured trip counts by site. Record the exact input, script and Python version. State whether blank measurements were excluded and whether zeros were retained. Save the count and sum for one group as an independent check. Rerun from a newly extracted copy to find files or assumptions accidentally left in the original workspace.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python First-Run Smoke Test
content:
Open the starter from **Core Project: Notebook Workflow and Reproducibility**. Run it without edits. The line `TODO: complete summarize` shows that Python started and reached the starter's placeholder. Record the runtime, input path, action or command, and the first output line.

Once you complete the earlier project, run it again on the supplied CSV. Check for six records, 32 total trips and a mean of 5.33. If the starter fails before the placeholder, record the first error and whether it concerns the runtime, an import or an input path. Adjust one setup detail and rerun.

module: Data Science in Python: Toolchain and Version Assumptions
title: Data Science in Python Version Drift Review
content:
Use one supplied CSV project in two supported environments, or compare one actual run with an earlier recorded run of the same starter and input. Record Python and the packages used. Check the input version, row count, one numeric result and any warnings so a package change can be distinguished from a changed dataset.

Keep a short table with the two environments, the expected value, each observed value and one decision. If the results differ, choose a small input that isolates the difference. If they agree, list the behavior the comparison established and one behavior it leaves unchecked.

title: Data Science in Python Project Ladder
content:
## Move from a checked input to an independent report

Start by describing a public or supplied dataset and calculating one result by hand. In the cleaning challenge, keep the original file and explain each rejection or repair. In the chart redesign, use the checked values to compare two displays. The trend project adds a time window and a fair comparison. The final story combines these skills around a question chosen by the author.

## Worked progression

Suppose two sites each report trip counts. First verify each site's count of measured rows. Next clean an invalid field and repeat the count. Compare sites in a chart with labeled units and note the number of measurements behind each value. Reuse those checks before reporting a difference between months.

title: Data Science in Python Checkpoints
content:
## Verify one result at a time

1. Name the observation unit, what each field measures, and how the input marks a missing value.
2. Reconcile the original, accepted and rejected rows after cleaning.
3. Calculate one group total or rate by hand and compare it with the program.
4. Check that the chart labels and caption describe the same filtered data.
5. Rerun the saved project with its recorded input and compare the result.

## Worked checkpoint

A table has five trip measurements: 0, blank, 4, 6 and an invalid value written as `n/a?`. With a rule that excludes the blank and invalid entry, three rows are measured. Their total is 10 and the mean is 10 ÷ 3. If the program reports two measured rows or a mean of 5, check whether it dropped the valid zero.

title: Data Science in Python Rubric
content:
## Use evidence to assess a report

| Criterion | Evidence to inspect |
| --- | --- |
| Question and coverage | A named population or time range, the unit of observation and a matching dataset |
| Cleaning and analysis | A data dictionary, logged exclusions and one independent calculation |
| Communication | A labeled table or chart, a claim supported by it and one consequence of a limitation |
| Reproducibility | The exact input, code and instructions needed to regenerate the result |

## Worked review

A caption says Service A was “used most often.” The chart shows trips per day, and the file has different numbers of observed days for each service. The chart supports a claim about rates over the observed days. It takes a separate total or equal coverage to support a claim about total use.

title: Data Science in Python Capstone Gate
content:
## Define an answerable first version

Write the audience, question, input, output and one previously checked calculation before building. Pick a normal case and a case that could expose a wrong result or a misleading display. List a fallback for a missing input or a tool that cannot run on the available device.

## Worked brief

A program coordinator needs to compare daily trips at two sites during one week. The first version uses a CSV with site, date and trips, checks coverage, and gives each site's daily rate and observation count. A hand calculation supplies the expected result for one site. A site with zero measured days produces an unavailable rate. A larger date range belongs in a later version once this one can be rerun.

title: Domain Projects Core Concepts
content:
## Match the question to the records

Name what one row represents, the measured quantities and who or what the records cover. A sports row might describe one team-game. A transit row can describe one route-week, with trips accumulated over a given number of observed days. Keep the observation unit and measurement units with each result.

## Worked transit example

North reports 20 trips over two days in Week 1 and 24 over four days in Week 2. The combined rate is (20 + 24) ÷ (2 + 4), or about 7.33 trips per covered day. Averaging the two weekly rates gives 8 because it gives each week equal weight. Choose the denominator that matches the question.

A missing trip count represents an unmeasured value. A report with zero trips and two covered days represents a measured rate of zero. Compare routes to describe differences between services, then group by week to check whether the same pattern appears across periods. Put the input, method, both views and a limitation into one report.

For an optional second domain, use the life expectancy dataset. Compare one country across years or compare two countries in the same year. Check which years and values are present before interpreting a trend.

title: Core Project: Domain Projects
content:
Open the starter for **Compare Trip Rates by Route and Week**. Use the supplied fictional transit CSV. Complete `summarize(reports, key)` to add trips and covered days separately within each group, then compute trips per covered day. Use the same function to make one view by route and another by week. Sort both views by label.

Check that North has 77 trips over nine days, about 8.56 trips per day. Week W2 has 45 trips over nine route-days, or 5.00 trips per route-day. Two routes measured on the same date contribute two route-days. Check that a file with only a blank trip count reports no measured rows.

Deliver the two views and a short statement identifying the observation unit, how a measured zero differs from a missing value, and one reason the observed rates may differ from rates for a full season.

title: Project: Simple Sort and Ranking Warmup
content:
Open the ranking starter. Practice selection sorting by repeatedly moving the next highest trips-per-day value into a new list. When rates tie, use route name order. The input is a list of tuples containing a route name, trips and positive covered days. Keep that list unchanged.

The sample shows North at 12 trips in three days and South at eight in two. Both rates equal four, so North comes before South. East follows them. Verify the order, the unchanged input and the output for an empty list. A pair such as 5 ÷ 3 and 10 ÷ 6 also ties. Use exact fractions when comparing rates before displaying decimals.

title: Transfer Practice: Domain Projects
content:
Open **Audit a Route-Week Dataset**. Complete `audit_reports(rows)` so each input row is either kept or assigned one rejection reason. Use the order in the starter README. The first valid record for a route-week stays. Return the kept route-weeks in input order and the counts by reason.

For the supplied file, reconcile ten rows to six kept and four rejected. Verify one count each for invalid data, missing trips, no coverage and duplicates. Then put an unmeasured row before a valid zero-trip row for the same route-week. The zero with observed days remains valid.

Keep the original input and report which rule decided each sample rejection. Explain what the duplicate count would mean if the dataset recorded several observations per route-week.

title: Extension Practice: Domain Projects
content:
Open **Check Sensitivity to Coverage**. Complete `compare_coverage(reports, minimum_days)` so each route has an overall rate and a rate using only reports with at least the chosen number of covered days. Include the number of reports behind each rate and report an unavailable result when all measured rows for a route are filtered out.

Use the default cutoff of three days. North changes from 8.56 to 8.14 trips per day and South stays at 6.50. East has a measured zero before the cutoff and an unavailable result afterward. Run a cutoff of one day and check that both columns agree.

Write which conclusions survived the coverage rule and why changes in the included records can change the reported rates without showing a change in demand.

module: Module 7: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
title: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit Core Concepts
content:
## Connect one control to one question

Altair describes how fields control chart properties. A site label is nominal, so map it to the category axis. A trip count is quantitative, so map it to bar length. Streamlit can present the chart in a web page and supply a selected site. With the default widget behavior, choosing a site reruns the script using the new value.

## Worked dashboard

Save this example as `app.py` in a Python environment with pandas, Altair and Streamlit. Run `python -m streamlit run app.py` from that folder. The example data are fictional.

```python
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

reports = pd.DataFrame({"site": ["North", "South"], "trips": [12, 8]})
site = st.selectbox("Site", ["All", "North", "South", "East"])
selected = reports if site == "All" else reports[reports["site"] == site]

if selected.empty:
    st.write("No matching reports")
else:
    st.metric("Observed trips", int(selected["trips"].sum()))
    st.altair_chart(
        alt.Chart(selected).mark_bar().encode(
            x=alt.X("site:N", title="Site"),
            y=alt.Y("trips:Q", title="Observed trips"),
        )
    )
```

The default view shows two bars and 20 trips. North shows one bar and 12 trips. East shows the no-match message. Check that the chart, count and caption use the same filtered rows in each state. These are total trips over the supplied observations. Comparing daily rates would require a day count for each site.

[Altair encodings](https://altair-viz.github.io/user_guide/encodings/index.html) · [Streamlit widget behavior](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior)

title: Data Science Capstone Core Concepts
content:
## Build an analysis that another reader can rerun

Start with a question the records can answer. Name the audience, input source, unit of observation and comparison window. Keep the raw input and document changes before calculating a metric. Save the code or notebook, the chart or table, and the exact command or steps needed to regenerate the result.

## Worked capstone check

A report compares trips per covered day at two sites. North records 24 trips over four days and South records 18 over three days. North has more recorded trips, yet both rates are six per day. Show both the count and the coverage so a reader can see why the comparisons differ. If a third site has no observed days, show its rate as unavailable.

A narrative notebook fits a fixed argument that benefits from explanation beside each step. A dashboard fits a question the audience answers by changing a filter. Whichever format is used, keep one hand calculation, one missing-data or empty-filter check, and a statement of what the result can support.

title: Practice Project: Public Dataset Exploratory Report
content:
Open the starter and complete `summarize(rows, start_year, end_year)`. Use `--year 2020` when checking the case with no overlapping observations.

Use the supplied six observations from the course life expectancy dataset. Compare Canada and Japan in the last observed year, then describe each country's change from 2013 to 2015. State that each row is one country-year and that the values measure life expectancy in years. Keep the original country and year labels.

In 2015 the values are 82.2 and 83.7, a difference of 1.5 years. The rounded changes from 2013 are 0.4 years for Canada and 0.2 years for Japan. Verify those values against the CSV and check what the report displays for a requested year outside the sample.

Deliver a small table, a source note, a chart or concise comparison, and one limitation. For extension, choose another set of country-year records and check their coverage before comparing them.

title: Practice Project: Messy CSV Cleaning Challenge
content:
Open the starter and complete `classify(rows)`. The program prints a clean CSV and rejection log that can each be saved as a separate file. Keep the original CSV for the reconciliation.

Keep a copy of the supplied station CSV. Read it with a CSV parser so the comma within “North, Annex” stays in one field. Accept a non-negative integer rider count, including zero. Keep the first valid record for each ID. Give every other row an outcome such as duplicate, missing count or invalid count.

The sample contains eight rows. Check that four are accepted, with 25 riders in total. The accepted rows include the measured zero. Deliver the clean rows and a rejection log with record ID and reason. Reconcile the two outputs to the original count.

Add one invalid row before a valid record with the same ID as a second check. Explain where the first valid record rule matters.

title: Practice Project: Visualization Redesign Project
content:
Open the starter and complete `draw_bars(observations)`. Use the same scale for both bars and keep the exact counts in their labels. Check an all-zero input as well as equal positive counts.

Compare two displays of the supplied trip counts. Service A has 42 and Service B has 49. A draft bar chart begins at 40, leaving bar lengths of 2 and 9. Calculate the difference of seven trips from the actual data and explain how the cropped baseline exaggerates it.

Redesign the chart using a zero baseline for the bars or a labeled dot plot that conveys position. Include a title, units and values a reader can verify. Use the same data in both displays and compare how each one answers the question.

Replace both sample values with the same count and verify that the redesign shows equality. Include an accessible text summary with the updated chart.

title: Practice Project: Weather, Sports, Transit, or Education Trend Analysis
content:
Open the starter and complete `compare_weeks(rows)`. Keep the source week order. A measured zero with positive coverage produces a zero rate, while a missing trip count produces an unavailable rate.

Use the supplied weekly transit observations as a starting case. Week 1 records 20 trips in two days and Week 2 records 30 in three days. Both rates are 10 per day. Week 3 has no measured trips and zero covered days. Week 4 records 36 in four days, or nine per day.

Create a labeled table of the weeks, observed counts, days and rates. Show the missing week as unavailable and leave a gap in any line that would imply a continuous observed trend. Explain why the change in raw counts can tell a different story from the change in rates.

Apply the same approach to a public weather, sports, transit or education series if a suitable input is available. State the time unit, measurement units and what a missing period means for that series.

title: Practice Project: Self-directed Final Data Story with Conclusions and Limitations
content:
Open the starter and complete `build_views(rows)` before adapting it to an independent question. The bundled example includes the Domain Projects data and adds a route with zero coverage. North has 77 trips over nine measured days, and West has an unavailable rate.

Choose a question and audience. Use the provided route-week data from Domain Projects or bring a documented dataset with suitable coverage. Write one claim supported by a table or chart and add a second view that checks it from another angle. For example, compare routes using trips per covered day, then show weekly coverage to explain how much evidence each comparison uses.

Deliver a script, notebook or dashboard that regenerates the two views. Include the exact input, one hand-checked value, a missing-data or filter check, the final claim and an important limitation. For the supplied transit fallback, a site with no covered days must display an unavailable rate.

Keep the question narrow enough that a reader can rerun the first version and identify which record or calculation supports the claim.

title: Build a Dashboard or Narrative Notebook
content:
Use the laptop-loan data from the core capstone or another documented dataset with the same question and coverage checks. Choose a dashboard when the audience needs to compare several selections. Choose a narrative notebook when the audience needs a fixed walk-through from input to conclusion.

For a dashboard, add a phase control with **Both**, **Before** and **After**. Show the selected phase, measured hours and loan rate together. With Both selected, the sample rates are 3.00 and 4.00 loans per measured hour. With Before selected, retain 14 measured hours and label the excluded week. Try a selection containing zero measured hours and replace the rate with an explanation.

For a notebook, order the cells as source and units, coverage check, grouped calculation, labeled comparison and conclusion. Restart the kernel and run every cell in order. The Before result is 42 loans over 14 measured hours. Verify that the narrative and chart show the same denominator.

Deliver the exact input and run instructions. Include the default result, one boundary check and the limit of the before-and-after comparison.

title: Core Project: Data Science Capstone
content:
Open **Compare Laptop Loan Rates** and complete `summarize(observations)`. The supplied fictional observations contain one phase-week per row. A zero loan count with positive observed hours is a measurement. A blank loan count or zero hours leaves that row outside the rate calculation. Preserve an exclusion count for each phase.

Use total measured loans divided by total measured hours. The sample Before phase has 42 loans and 14 hours, or 3.00 per hour. After has 60 loans and 15 hours, or 4.00 per hour. Run the project to produce `report.md`. Check one value by hand and verify that the saved table and console agree.

Run a second input where one phase lacks measured hours. Confirm that the report omits the numeric comparison and names the coverage limit. Submit the code, exact input, reproducible report and one reason the observed rate difference cannot establish the effect of the pilot.

title: Transfer Practice: Data Science Capstone
content:
Open **Verify a Data Revision**. Complete `changes(previous, revised)` to report added and removed phase-week records and field changes. Compare the two supplied snapshots by their phase and week keys. The output records the exact file fingerprints without changing the input.

In the default example, the After W3 loan count changes from 8 to 11. Total After loans rise from 60 to 63 while measured hours stay at 15. Check that the reported rate changes from 4.00 to 4.20. Reorder the original rows in a copy and compare it to the original. Its file fingerprint changes while its record comparison reports no changes.

Deliver both file versions, the changed-field log and a sentence naming which result needs rechecking before reusing the report.

title: Extension Practice: Data Science Capstone
content:
Open **Stress-Test Coverage**. Complete `coverage_summary(observations, minimum_hours)` so both phases use the same minimum. Compare the baseline of one hour with the default threshold of seven. For each phase, display the remaining measured rows and hours beside the recalculated rate.

With seven hours, the Before rate stays at 3.00 while measured hours fall from 14 to 8. The After rate increases from 4.00 to 4.86 while its measured hours fall from 15 to 7. Check that a threshold of nine makes both rates unavailable. Cite the remaining hours when interpreting any difference.

Deliver both settings, the two comparison outputs and a conclusion explaining how the stricter rule changes the amount of evidence available.

module: Module 7: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
title: Core Project: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
content:
Open **Compare Room Check-ins by Day** and complete `summarize_day(rows, day)`. The fictional dataset contains one room and day per row. Calculate the total from exactly the selected rows and reuse those rows for the chart and table.

The IDE runs the calculation in `main.py`. Monday contains 6 Quiet and 12 Studio check-ins, totaling 18. Change the command's default day to Tuesday in the IDE or run `python main.py --day Tuesday` locally. Tuesday includes an observed zero for Quiet and 9 arrivals at Studio. Check both totals by hand.

Follow the README to launch `dashboard.py` with Streamlit locally. Use the Day control and check that the Altair chart, table, total and caption change together. Deliver evidence of both day selections and explain that repeat visits contribute to check-in counts.

module: Module 7: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
title: Transfer Practice: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
content:
Open **Distinguish Empty Filters from Zero** and complete `filter_observations(rows, day, room)`. Match the selected day and room. The All rooms selection applies the day filter while retaining every room observed that day.

In the IDE, run the default view and change the default Day and Room values to test two boundaries. Tuesday Quiet has a measured count of zero. Wednesday Quiet has no matching observation. In the local dashboard, confirm that the first case retains a table and chart and the second shows a clear unavailable message.

Switch the Room control from Quiet to All rooms while keeping Wednesday selected. Studio's four check-ins appear in the chart, table and total. Save evidence of all three states and explain the coverage represented by each.

module: Module 7: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
title: Extension Practice: Dashboards with Altair and Streamlit
content:
Open **Keep a Common Scale for Day Comparisons** and complete `comparable_panels(rows, first_day, second_day)`. Filter the days independently and obtain the common upper limit from the full dataset. The bundled data gives both charts a range of 0 to 12 observed check-ins.

Run the calculation in the IDE and compare Monday with Tuesday. Then use the native dashboard controls to compare Tuesday with Wednesday. Wednesday's Studio value is 4, and both charts retain the 0 to 12 range. Check that each table lists only the observed rooms for its selected day.

Submit both filtered tables, the two chart views, and a sentence explaining why a common scale makes values comparable. Repeat with an all-zero sample and verify that the chart domain retains room to display zero.
